after.problem:
Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=2(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,y=2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,t\in [0,\pi ].

after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =2t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(2t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4{t}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\cdot {\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =2(\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}-0) \\  & ={\pi }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(2(sin⁡t−tcos⁡t))=2cos⁡t−2(cos⁡t−tsin⁡t)=2tsin⁡t and dydt=ddt(2(cos⁡t+tsin⁡t))=−2sin⁡t+2(sin⁡t+tcos⁡t)=2tcos⁡t.

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫0π(2tsin⁡t)2+(2tcos⁡t)2dt=∫0π4t2(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)dt=2∫0πtdt=2⋅t22|0π=2(π22−0)=π2.

decision.explanation: For a parametric curve, L=∫₀¹√((x'(t))²+(y'(t))²) dt. Here x'(t)=1/2 and y'(t)=e^t, so L=∫₀¹√(1/4+e^(2t)) dt=(1/2)∫₀¹√(4e^(2t)+1) dt, which is option a.

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=\frac{t}{2},\,y={e}^{t}$
from $t=0$ to $t=1$ (shown above)?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have
We have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t}{2})=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{({e}^{2t})+(\frac{1}{4})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{4{e}^{2t}+1}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=\frac{t}{2},\,y={e}^{t}$
from $t=0$ to $t=1$ (shown above)?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have
We have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t}{2})=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{({e}^{2t})+(\frac{1}{4})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{4{e}^{2t}+1}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The arc length is ∫₀²√((x'(t))²+(y'(t))²) dt. Since x'(t)=e^t and y'(t)=1, this becomes ∫₀²√(e^(2t)+1) dt, matching option c.

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={e}^{t},\,y=t$
from $t=0$ to $t=2$ (shown above)?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{({e}^{t})^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+1}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={e}^{t},\,y=t$
from $t=0$ to $t=2$ (shown above)?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{({e}^{t})^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+1}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+4t)=4,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{8}{3}{t}^{3/2})=4{t}^{1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{(4{t}^{1/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{16+16t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2}(1+t)^{1/2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\cdot \frac{2}{3}(1+t)^{3/2}\,{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}({3}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}(3\sqrt{3}-1) \\  & =8\sqrt{3}-\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
